    • According to recent reports, on November 8, 2026, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) reportedly re-arrested Haroun, interior minister of Sudan in 2007, when an ICC arrest warrant was issued against him.
    • In a recent development, “For two decades, victims of atrocity crimes in Darfur have witnessed Haroun and others evading justice, leading to impunity-fueled cycles of violence that are claiming more victims every day.” noted Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (The Hague) – Sudanese authorities should immediately transfer former Interior Minister Ahmed Haroun to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to face charges in The Hague, Human Rights Watch stated today. Haroun was recently taken into Sudanese custody and faces ICC war crimes and crimes against humanity charges, committed in Sudan’s Darfur region, in 2003 and 2004.

    According to recent reports, on November 8, 2026, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) reportedly re-arrested Haroun, interior minister of Sudan in 2007, when an ICC arrest warrant was issued against him. He was arrested one day after he took part in a video podcast interview, his first public appearance since 2019. The armed forces have not officially confirmed Haroun’s whereabouts, but media reported that he is detained in Khartoum state.

    In a recent development, “For two decades, victims of atrocity crimes in Darfur have witnessed Haroun and others evading justice, leading to impunity-fueled cycles of violence that are claiming more victims every day.” noted Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “If Sudan’s authorities transferred those sought by the ICC to the court in The Hague, as they are obliged to do, it would send a powerful message to those committing crimes today that they too may find themselves in the dock.”.

    Authorities should also transfer former President Omar al-Bashir—who is believed to be in Sudanese custody in Khartoum state as well—and locate, arrest, and transfer former Defense Minister Abdelrahim M. Hussein. The ICC has also issued arrest warrants for both of them, though there is no information available on Hussein’s location.

    According to recent reports, the ICC issued an arrest warrant against Haroun in 2007, and another against Hussein in 2012, for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2004. During that period, Sudanese government forces and allied militias carried out targeted attacks against civilians on the basis of their ethnicity, including killings, rape, forced displacement from their homes and land, and burning of their villages. In 2009 and 2010, the ICC issued two arrest warrants against al-Bashir for alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2008.

    Following al-Bashir’s ouster in April 2019, Sudanese authorities held Haroun, al-Bashir, and Hussein in custody for charges not related to atrocities in Darfur but failed to transfer them to the ICC.

    After fighting erupted between SAF and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on April 15, 2023, the authorities moved al-Bashir to Alia military hospital in Omdurman, Khartoum state, where he reportedly remained under guard, while Haroun left detention amid the collapse of prison security, and under circumstances suggesting coordination with judicial authorities.

    Recent findings suggest that on September 30, 2026, SAF granted al-Bashir initial approval to travel outside of Sudan for medical treatment. Based on media reports, al-Bashir continues to receive medical care at Alia military hospital and is yet to travel abroad.

    UN Security Council Resolution 1593, referring the situation in Darfur to the ICC prosecutor, requires the government of Sudan to cooperate with the court even though it is not a party to the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty. In 2021, the ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor signed a memorandum of understanding with the Sudanese authorities addressing cooperation for arrests. The ICC lacks the ability to enforce its own orders and relies on state cooperation to conduct investigations and make arrests.

    In January and July, the Office of the Prosecutor reported to the United Nations Security Council on its investigation in Darfur, including its continued engagement with Sudanese authorities. In addition to addressing crimes from July 2002 onward, the Office of the Prosecutor is also investigating crimes committed since April 2023 in Darfur. The prosecutor’s office reported “positive” and “significant” cooperation by Sudanese authorities, and assistance in support of its investigative activities, including deployment of the office’s investigative team to Port Sudan.

    According to recent reports, nevertheless, Sudan has not fulfilled its obligation to carry out the court’s arrest warrants and transfer the wanted suspects to the Hague. The authorities should provide public information on the whereabouts of all the wanted suspects and take immediate steps to allow their transfer to the court, Human Rights Watch noted.

    The African Union, the members of the Atrocity Prevention and Justice Coalition for Sudan–– particularly the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Sierra Leone––as well as the European Union and its member states should directly engage with Sudanese authorities, calling on them to comply with their obligation to fully cooperate with the ICC and to transfer Haroun, al-Bashir, and Hussein to the court’s custody.

    Sources indicate that ICC judges have referred to the Security Council several findings of noncooperation against Sudan and ICC member states in relation to the arrest of ICC suspects. However, the council has never taken steps to enforce these findings. UN member states should urge the Security Council to back the ICC’s mandate in Darfur, including by enforcing the court’s findings of noncooperation on arrests.

    The ICC prosecutor’s office should use its next biannual report to the council, in January 2027, as an opportunity to raise any concerns related to Sudan’s cooperation on arrests.

    Industry observers note that in 2025, the ICC convicted Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman (also known as Ali Kosheib), a former leader of Sudan’s “Janjaweed” militias, for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur in 2003 and 2004, and sentenced him to 20 years in prison. Kosheib’s trial was possible after he surrendered himself voluntarily to the ICC’s custody in 2020.

    “For victims and survivors of crimes in Darfur, Sudanese authorities’ promises of cooperation mean little without concrete action,” Evenson said. “Sudan’s international partners should use every diplomatic tool at their disposal to press for the immediate transfer of all ICC suspects in Sudanese custody and make clear that cooperation with the court is not optional.”.

    #32249. Tech Report: Andrew H. Murray on thrillers, the Booker, and taking comedy seriously in literature

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1278 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Andrew H. Murray on thrillers, the Booker, and taking comedy seriously in literature

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The UK has just recovered from Booker Prize Fever—alright, not so much a fever as a very, very slightly raised temperature–but in the last week there was a fair bit of interest in this massive and prestigious book award, mainly because the winner’s sales always go right to the moon.
    • My favorite of the books on the shortlist and the one I hoped would win was the terrific Black Bag.
    • I wanted Black Bag to win because I myself make my books funny as well as serious—I can’t help it—and my characters have senses of humor.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The UK has just recovered from Booker Prize Fever—alright, not so much a fever as a very, very slightly raised temperature–but in the last week there was a fair bit of interest in this massive and prestigious book award, mainly because the winner’s sales always go right to the moon.

    My favorite of the books on the shortlist and the one I hoped would win was the terrific Black Bag. It’s a mad story about a young out-of-work actor who is paid to wear a huge black bag and attend university lectures as part of a psychological experiment. Things rapidly get very weird; it’s a very funny book. But when awards night rolled around, in my opinion the jokes in it were far likelier to kneecap its chances than to help it over the line.

    I wanted Black Bag to win because I myself make my books funny as well as serious—I can’t help it—and my characters have senses of humor. My new book, Everything Happens So Much, is a story about why life feels so strange and difficult, and about why we’re all spending our one wonderful life comparing ourselves to strangers online who are supposedly having much better lives than us.

    According to recent reports, the main character of Everything Happens So Much, Esme, goes to hell and back. She’s put through the wringer. And yet, despite all the Deep Trauma she undergoes, the story has jokes in it, and the jokes are some of the bits I’m proudest of.

    No matter. Across the board in mainstream culture, there is a feeling that if you put jokes in, you can’t possibly do the serious stuff as well. Comedy demonstrates are written off as trivial, lightweight, split off into their own genre at the non-award-winning end of the room. When did a really funny film last win Best Picture?

    As a result, many writers who do comedy but aspire to mainstream success try to hide the fact. Black Bag has been sold on its chin-stroking lessons about masculinity, rather than its very good one-liners about life as an unemployed actor.

    It has been revealed that another of my other favorite authors right now writing is Mick Herron, author of the terrific Slough House set of thrillers. The Slough House books are set in a crew of failed spies, the agents who’ve wrecked their careers by leaving a secret document on the bus or screwing up a training exercise or simply being too unpleasant to work with.

    According to recent reports, in the hands of an unfunny author the books could have been an unremitting trudge through concrete canyons under grey skies. But Herron, and his characters, are funny. They are biting and cynical and everyone talks like they’ve been written for Apple TV. It’s not unconnected to this that they have been turned into umpteen series for Apple TV.

    Industry observers note that and is this comedy element of the books made obvious to the casual viewer? It is not. The covers are serious, the straplines are serious, they’re sold on their thrills. There aren’t many blurbs from other authors about how hilarious the books are. But when you read them, as well as being swept along by the plots, you laugh.

    In a recent development, in my own case, I can’t help it. I started out writing for QI, the British panel show, where the aim is to tell people the most interesting facts in the funniest possible way. The whole show is an exercise in ‘education by stealth’, on the principle that if you’re laughing, you won’t realize you’re learning.

    Sources indicate that I then cofounded the podcast No Such Thing As A Fish, which has the same aim. I write for Private Eye magazine—imagine The Onion, but topical. I’m well aware of what you have to do to sell a book these days, though, and it’s this: lie your head off about whether you’re trying to be funny.

    Why is there this snootiness towards comedy? In my view comedy is much harder to write than the serious stuff. Pathos is simply a matter of making things sadder, which any fool can manage. Just give Tiny Tim one more disease or make Anna Karenina’s life that smidge worse: instant tragedy!

    According to recent reports, what’s hard is doing a good tight one-paragraph about life as a nineteenth-century serf which will have your reader laughing until they can’t breathe. (This, incidentally, is why Tolstoy was never given his own HBO special.).

    According to recent reports, but the myth persists that funny can’t coexist along with serious, despite all the evidence from our lives that it is in the most serious moments that we are most in need of our senses of humor. When I talk about Everything Happens So Much—to remind you, my newly introduced book which is available now—even I fall prey to this terrible effect.

    Recent findings suggest that I shouldn’t even be admitting this to you. I should be amping up the elements of existential angst. But, honestly, the book contains jokes interwoven with the existential angst, and there’s nothing I can do about it.

    According to recent reports, maybe this defensiveness about comedy in most media is because everyone is aware that it yields rewards. Comedians sell out stadiums, they get specials, the clips of their crowd work or their sketches absolutely saturate most media. Why the hell should they have the book market stitched up too?

    But I think the real reason is that jokes are binary—you either get them or you don’t—and the truth is that it’s almost impossible to write a book which will appeal to everyone. All our lives are different, and so all the things we laugh at will be slightly different too. We can all agree that the ending of Of Mice And Men is a tearjerker; if it had ended with Lenny and George doing a tight five at a local comedy club, only about half the readership would have found it funny.

    The real truth, though, is that funny is the caramel which only heightens the salt. We live in this world, with all its absurdities and tragedies, and yet we know that life is a comedy even if sometimes we watch it through tears. Comedy and tragedy prop each other up and help each other towards the finish line. A novel of pure comedy would be far too light; a purely tragic novel would be too grim to finish. (Thomas Hardy, I’m looking at you.).

    So if you yourself write funny, if you can’t help it, if a sense of humor keeps breaking out despite your best intentions, then for goodness’ sake embrace it. Know and appreciate your amazing power.

    According to recent reports, but my only advice is this: don’t let on. And don’t, whatever you do, write an entire article confessing your fresh book, which is available now, is extremely funny as well as poignant and thought-provoking. It will do sales no good whatsoever.

    Everything Happens So Much is available to buy now.

    Andrew H. Murray is an author, broadcaster and comedian. He cohosts the award-winning podcast No Such Thing As a Fish, which is one of the top 10 podcasts in the UK and has been downloaded 500 million times, as well as BBC Radio 4's satirical news program The Naked Week. He writes jokes and journalism for Private Eye (think: a hybrid of The Onion and The Nation). He is the author of Everything Happens So Much. Murray lives in London.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, james Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

    Ashbacher was charged by an indictment unsealed Tuesday with unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information and with theft of government property.

    According to the indictment, beginning in or about 2021, the defendant worked as an employee of a private firm that provided security and emergency management services at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command facility in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. To perform the required functions of his employment, Ashbacher held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

    As further detailed in the indictment, Ashbacher photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other people to a second social media site. Ashbacher asked a social media user in a private message to remove some materials and further stated that he was “trying to do some damage control.” A search of Ashbacher’s residence also revealed a classified award write-up that contained additional national defense information, along with a night vision goggle system specific to a military unit within Army Special Operations Command that had been reported missing.

    The FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

    It has been revealed that trial Attorney Leslie Esbrook of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Logan Liles for the Eastern District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

    According to recent reports, an indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

    #32246. Breaking news: a new James Bond has been chosen!

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1128 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking news: a new James Bond has been chosen!

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that friends, gather round!
    • The new James Bond has been revealed!!
    • Industry observers note that there has been much, much speculation about who would be the upcoming Bond—the eighth actor to play Bond (in a legitimate adaptation… go away, 1967’s Casino Royale), and the star of the twenty-sixth Bond film.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that friends, gather round! There is news!

    The new James Bond has been revealed!! Finally, after five years of waiting (since Daniel Craig departed the franchise with/in 2021’s sentimental No Time to Die), we have a new 007.

    Industry observers note that there has been much, much speculation about who would be the upcoming Bond—the eighth actor to play Bond (in a legitimate adaptation… go away, 1967’s Casino Royale), and the star of the twenty-sixth Bond film. Would it be Slow Horses‘s Jack Lowden? Perhaps Josh O’Connor or Callum Turner? What about a dark horse, like CrimeReads favorite Josh Bowman? Remember way back when, when we all thought it would be Idris Elba? And remember how after that, we all thought it would be Aaron Taylor-Johnson?

    It has been revealed that nope! Turns out, the next James Bond will be….

    Yes, Robert Pattinson, the creative and hardworking English actor who will likely be nominated for a Supporting Actor Academy Award for his role as Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, this year. Robert Pattinson! Robert Pattinson is Bond!

    Industry observers note that the Bond franchise has the power to catapult an actor from a lesser-known realm into wild international fame. As I wrote previously,.

    The individuals I refer to as the James Bond Selection Committee chose Daniel Craig last time; a well-respected actor of stage and screen, known mostly for supporting roles. The point of Bond casting is not to choose someone so closely associated with another leading man role that it becomes distracting; the actor must fully embody Bond.

    This time, the selection committee chose Mr. Franchise, himself! Cedric Diggory of Harry Potter, Edward Cullen of Twilight (no matter how hard he tries to forget it), and Batman of The Batman! He’s about to be in Dune: Part III.

    Sources indicate that pattinson, who is 40, has worked with countless extraordinary filmmakers in many challenging parts, distancing himself from the heartthrobby roles he played in his youth. He has already lead films directed by David Cronenberg, Claire Denis, Bong Joon Ho, Werner Herzog, the Safdie Brothers, Robert Eggers, James Gray, Lynne Ramsay, Christopher Nolan, Fernando Meirelles, and Denis Villeneuve (who will be directing the next Bond film).

    Sources indicate that normally the James Bond persona subsumes the actor… the actor becomes Bond and always remains Bond, no matter what else he does. But Pattinson is so well-known already for his esoteric roles and big-budget blockbuster starring turns, and he himself has played so many famous characters, that this time (for the first time, I dare say), it’s the other way around.

    Ben Roberts, the CEO of the British Film Institute (BFI), noted this, remarking, “He’s a different kind of choice… he comes to the table with a huge amount of baggage, adding that the “amazing thing about Robert Pattinson is his ability to be a chameleon in his roles.”.

    It has been revealed that personally, I think Pattinson is an extraordinarily skilled performer, one who manages to put a creative and memorable take on even the most generic or hard-worn characters. He’s certainly one of the best actors of his generation. I’m sure that he will be a fabulous Bond, even though I am admittedly surprised by the decision. Pattinson won’t let us down, that I know.

    It has been revealed that well, this news also means that Matt Reeves’s sequel to his noirish 2022 masterpiece The Batman, titled The Batman: Part II, will probably be the end of that Batman series. I (and others) cannot imagine Pattinson doing a whole Batman performance in between James Bond performances. But… who knows? He’s a wild guy.

    It has been revealed that still, Bond is a very demanding role. Just look at what poor Daniel Craig suffered through!

    According to The New York Times,.

    Pattinson was chosen over Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. The five actors underwent screen tests in London in late October. The auditions involved stunts, dialogue and camera presence; they were overseen by Nina Gold, an Oscar-nominated (“Hamnet”) and Emmy-winning (“Game of Thrones”) casting director. Bond auditions can be revealing: Henry Cavill, who lost the role to Craig in the previous casting search, told Men’s Health in 2019 that he was asked to re-enact a scene in which Sean Connery’s Bond emerged from a bathroom in nothing but a towel.

    Notably, however, this is the first James Bond film that will proceed without the famed Broccoli family/EON productions at the helm, ending their six-decade-long stewardship of the brand. In 2022, the tech giant Amazon acquired 50 percent control over the Bond property as part of its 2022 purchase of MGM (for $8.5 billion). Barbara Broccoli and her half-brother Michael G. Wilson, who inherited the rights from her father Albert R. “Cubby” Broccoli upon his passing in 1996, had retained the other 50 percent, and had been guaranteed a final say on virtually everything. They had “ironclad creative control, deciding when to make a newly introduced Bond film, who should play the title role and whether remakes and television spinoffs got made” and “also had final say over every line of dialogue, every casting decision, every stunt sequence, every marketing tie-in, as well as every TV ad, poster and billboard.”.

    But in February 2025, after reported longstanding creative tensions between Barbara and Amazon, Barbara agreed to transfer creative control to Amazon. Wilson and Broccoli have chosen more passive roles. They will remain co-owners of the franchise, but are relinquishing all creative control to Amazon. In March 2025, it was revealed that Harry Potter producer David Heyman would be in charge of the Bond property for Amazon, along with Amy Pascal. Their companies Heyday Films and Pascal Pictures, would produce the future Bond installments.

    Almost nothing else is known about this next Bond film, except that the screenplay will be an original story (as there are no more of Ian Fleming’s Bond stories to adapt), written by Steven Knight, the creator of the series Peaky Blinders.

    Sources indicate that stay tuned for more updates… and in the meantime, congratulations to Robert Pattinson! Cheers!

    #32245. Why the American West Is the Perfect Setting for a Crime Novel

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1095 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Why the American West Is the Perfect Setting for a Crime Novel

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1095 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Before we can answer the question of why the American West is the perfect place for a crime story, we need to clarify what the American West is.
    • For purposes of crime fiction, I propose that the American West should be considered any place that meets all five of the following criteria:.
    • In a recent development, I’m not kidding.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Before we can answer the question of why the American West is the perfect place for a crime story, we need to clarify what the American West is. This is necessary because there seems to be a great deal of confusion on the subject. You can see this in almost any man-on-the-street interview which quickly reveals that the average American’s understanding of geography is less a body of knowledge than it is a collection of strangely confident opinions. For instance, people who live where I do, in Nevada, might look at Boston, Fresh York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Washington and think, “You people are practically sharing a driveway.” Similarly, many people who live along the Eastern Seaboard believe that anything west of the Mississippi River qualifies as the West.

    For purposes of crime fiction, I propose that the American West should be considered any place that meets all five of the following criteria:.

    (1) It’s a Place Where Nobody Can Hear You Scream.

    In a recent development, I’m not kidding. The West has a lot of empty space. In Tallahassee or Atlanta, if someone screams at 2:17 a.m., seventeen people call 911. In Nevada, there may not be another person within 47 miles. This is both atmospheric and convenient for murder. And for crime authors. The amount of open space is incomprehensible to people who live in tighter confines and where the horizon often consists of a strip mall, a water tower and a billboard advertising personal injury attorneys.

    Recent findings suggest that now, don’t get me wrong. There are a lot of desolate areas out here. But while there might not be any humans within earshot of your scream, rest assured the coyotes, wolves, bears, and other high school mascots can hear you. When you scream in the West, be careful, lest you inadvertently ring the dinner bell for some other kind of serial killer.

    (2) It’s a Place Where You Can Hide a Body Almost Anywhere.

    In a recent development, when human remains are discovered in urban areas, there’s a good chance they’ve haven’t been hidden for more than ten minutes. That’s because there’s no good place to dispose of them without being caught on someone’s cell phone video. If you hope to hide your victim, you have to have a space in grandma’s wall or have a large, airtight cooler. In the West, you have deserts and mountains, some with places where no human has ever left a track. You have canyons so vast that the chances of finding a body begin to depend more on plate tectonics than police work. You have ghost towns with mine shafts so deep that any body placed in one will have to be carbon-dated if and when it’s ever found.

    (3) It’s a Place Where Everyone Has a Truck.

    Sources indicate that this solves an enormous number of plot problems for western crime authors. Need to transport a body? Truck. Need to follow someone into the wilderness? Truck. Need your protagonist to spend three chapters driving while contemplating the meaning of life? Truck.

    Recent findings suggest that why does everyone in the American West have a truck, you ask? Because daily life demands one. Just watch any of those YouTube channels featuring people who camp in places a normal vehicle could never get to. I’m convinced many of these YouTube campers are serial killers. Also, in a lot of places, there are so few people that everybody knows everybody, so any crime committed has to be hidden where the eyes of prying neighbors aren’t focused. To get there, you need a truck. Trust me.

    (4) It’s a Place Where Everyone Owns a Gun.

    As a writer of crime fiction, this is particularly useful because you can eliminate several pages of explanation.

    According to recent reports, in the American West, there are more guns than there are people. Most people own multiple firearms, and children are introduced to them shortly after learning to walk. Sometimes earlier. You may argue the merits of this…until little Tommy uses that .22 you bought him to shoot the rattlesnake that’s about to bite his sister. If, some years later, Tommy turns that same rifle on a person, well, that’s the makings of a pretty good crime story.

    (5) It’s Place That Gives Your Detective Something Beautiful to Look at While Brooding.

    And this is, perhaps, the most vital thing. The West is practically a literary service.

    Mountain ranges. Sunsets. Deserts. Snow. Massive sky. Canyons.

    A detective in the West is never more than a few minutes away from something worth staring at while contemplating a murder, a missing person, a regrettable decision or the general decline of civilization.

    In a recent development, try doing that on the Jersey Turnpike. A detective there walks outside, looks dramatically into the distance and sees a Wawa.

    The West gives a crime novelist something even more than just scenery: space. Space for a crime to happen. Space for a secret to survive. Space for a suspect to disappear. Space for a sheriff to chase him. And, most importantly, space for a character to stand on a ridge at sunset and wonder what the hell happened to his life.

    For me, geography is everything. It’s as much a character in my novels as my protagonist, Porter Beck. When I build an outline for a newly introduced story, I plot the scenery just as I do my character biographies. I plot the time of year, the colors, the smells, the flora and fauna. In some cases – most actually – the physical setting is as much an adversary to Beck as the person he’s trying to stop. It might be snow drifts or wildfires or the relentless summer heat.

    Sources indicate that it’s the opportunities this landscape provides that make the American West the perfect place to stage a crime novel. Out here, there is room for everything a crime story needs.

    BRUCE BORGOS lives and writes from the Nevada desert where he works hard every day to prove his high school guidance counselor had good instincts when he said “You’ll never be an astronaut.” He has a degree in political science which mostly served to dissuade him from a career in law while at the same time tormenting his wife with endless questions about how telephones work. When not writing, you can usually find him at the local wine store. He is the author of The Bitter Past.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fbi ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S.
    • Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.
    • “Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” mentioned Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.

    Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.

    “Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” mentioned Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”.

    “For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”.

    “Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”.

    “Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” remarked Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”.

    According to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.

    Industry observers note that much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.

    During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.

    Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.

    It has been revealed that on some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”.

    According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.

    It has been revealed that the FBI Washington Field Office investigated the case, with assistance from the U.S. Department of State's Diplomatic Security Service.

    Recent findings suggest that the matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.

    • British comedian and actor Russell Brand was sentenced in London on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison following his conviction for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.
    • High Court of England and Wales Judge Joel Bennathan described Brand, 51, as a sexual predator who used his public standing to shield himself from accountability before women came forward following media reports in 2023, Courthouse News Service reports.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    British comedian, actor and podcaster Russell Brand arrives at the Southwark Crown Court in London during his trial on charges of rape, sexual assault and indecent assault. He was convicted and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    British comedian and actor Russell Brand was sentenced in London on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison following his conviction for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

    High Court of England and Wales Judge Joel Bennathan described Brand, 51, as a sexual predator who used his public standing to shield himself from accountability before women came forward following media reports in 2023, Courthouse News Service reports.

    Brand will likely serve two-thirds of his sentence before being released on parole, the judge noted. The sentencing followed a four-week trial in which jurors found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

    Before the sentencing, the court heard victim impact statements from the women, who described the lasting effects of the attacks on their confidence, relationships and ability to feel safe.

    The judge considered Brand’s charitable work, including helping people struggling with addiction by funding treatment. However, he stated good character and exemplary conduct would not normally justify a significant reduction in a prison sentence.

    Rhys Bowen on writing real people and settings in historical fiction

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, one of the aspects of the Royal Spyness series that readers like is that it involves the British royal family in the 1930s.
    • It has been revealed that introducing real people to my plots is a bit of a risk, I suppose, but I am by no means unique.
    • In a recent development, when I started the series I had to think how far I wanted to go from what we know of these characters and I decided I wanted to keep as close as possible to what I knew they said and felt.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, one of the aspects of the Royal Spyness series that readers like is that it involves the British royal family in the 1930s. The Prince of Wales, Mrs. Simpson the king and queen, the little princesses walk across the pages and are part of the plots. Other well-known real characters also are featured: Coco Chanel in a couple of books, Noel Coward in several and even Agatha Christie helps solve a mystery in From Cradle to Grave. My fictional heroine is supposedly related to the royals, a great granddaughter of Queen Victoria and thus a cousin first cousin once removed to the Prince of Wales.

    It has been revealed that introducing real people to my plots is a bit of a risk, I suppose, but I am by no means unique. Shakespeare certainly wrote about plenty of real people but he retold their true lives. Taking a real person and putting them into a fictional plot is a little different. It is stretching truth and not everybody will be happy with that.

    In a recent development, when I started the series I had to think how far I wanted to go from what we know of these characters and I decided I wanted to keep as close as possible to what I knew they said and felt. Queen Mary was a stickler for rules and passionate about antiques so in one plot I had her charge my heroine with reclaiming an antique that had been stolen from her.

    Recent findings suggest that I suppose the one person I took the most liberties with was Mrs. Simpson. Since I knew she had a sharp tongue and could be very cruel I enjoyed making her quite unpleasant for several books until she ends up helping my heroine.

    Recent findings suggest that using real people and real settings requires a lot of research. I have to confess that I have poked into every corner of Buckingham Palace, and Kensington Palace, read all the biographies of Chanel and Noel Coward, the Prince of Wales and Mrs Simpson. To me it is important to recreate a real person as faithfully as possible.

    In writing about real people each author has to decide how far they want to go and in what ways they might deviate from truth. Some writers have taken real people and made them sleuths. Stephanie Baron made Jane Austen (very successfully) into a sleuth. Karen Harper had  Queen Elizabeth I solve crimes. Gyles Brandreth makes Oscar Wilde a detective.

    In a recent development, did any of these people really have time to do a little detecting on the side? And without being observed? Jane Austen clearly could have been a good sleuth with her powers of observation of the human condition, especially as she would have been overlooked, sitting in a corner as an unmarried woman. But Queen Elizabeth was accompanied every second of the day. Could she have found time and opportunity to sleuth a little?

    So is the writer allowed to take real people and make them do things they didn’t do? Is there a chance of getting sued? Apparently not if they were a public figure. I could include Agatha Christie in my book, doing what she did best…solve a crime. But I don’t know about making them do something they would never have done: make them a murderer? I think the family would have cause to bring a lawsuit if a respectable person was defamed.

    I don’t think I would be comfortable with making a real person do things I know they didn’t do. In fact it gives me great pleasure in having real characters say things I knew they really mentioned. It’s like weaving reality and fiction together.

    According to recent reports, my favorite example is when Lady Georgie meets her cousins Princess Elizabeth and Princess Margaret. Margaret is three at the time. Georgie claims “Hello Margaret,” and Margaret replies, “You have to say Princess Margaret because I’m a princess.” To this Georgie says, “Then you have to say Lady Georgie to me because I’m a lady.”.

    Margaret looks up at her governess and asks, “Is a lady better than a princess?” To which her governess replies, “One hopes a princess will grow up to be a lady.” True story!

    For me the appeal of using real characters and putting my fictional heroine into a real world is that it immediately gives her credibility. It justifies her existence. She’s moving through a real society so we now believe she is real. We know all about Edward VIII and Mrs Simpson and we see Lady Georgie interacting with them. So we accept Lady Georgie as real. Very satisfying.

    As well as involving real people in my stories I have introduced real events. We were at Sandringham for the last days of King George V. We were with Mrs Simpson when the king decided to abdicate.

    According to recent reports, in this latest book in the Royal Spyness series, To Crown It All (book twenty!) the whole story centers around a real event: the coronation of King George and Queen Elizabeth in 1937. This was a well-documented event,  It was even filmed. So I made sure I kept every element completely accurate (except for a minor detail of a plot nobody knew about…which might have happened).

    I reasoned that my heroine, Lady Georgie, who is the king’s cousin, would be invited to the Abbey and be involved in the coronation, but I didn’t expect her to get so very involved!

    I find it very satisfying to recreate real history, to take readers back to a real time and place, but with the slight addition of my fictional sleuth.

    Rhys Bowen is the New York Times bestselling author of more than sixty novels, including Mrs. Endicott’s Splendid Adventure, The Rose Arbor, The Paris Assignment, Where the Sky Begins, The Venice Sketchbook, Above the Bay of Angels, The Victory Garden, The Tuscan Child, and In Farleigh Field, the winner of the Lefty Award for Best Historical Mystery Novel and the Agatha Award for Best Historical Novel. Bowen’s work has won sixteen honors to date, including multiple Agatha, Anthony, and Macavity Awards. Her books have been translated into many languages, and she has fans around the world, including more than seventy thousand Facebook followers. A transplanted Brit, Bowen divides her time between California and Arizona. For more information, visit www.rhysbowen.com.

    #32240. 7 mysteries that focus on the motive behind crimes

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1187 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    7 mysteries that focus on the motive behind crimes

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, means, motive, opportunity: they comprise the classic triad of mystery fiction.
    • For two decades before I wrote my debut novel, On the Killer’s Trail, I worked in education and libraries.
    • Here are seven novels that focus on motive in a variety of ways.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, means, motive, opportunity: they comprise the classic triad of mystery fiction. Of the three features, I appreciate motive as the real heart of a mystery story.

    For two decades before I wrote my debut novel, On the Killer’s Trail, I worked in education and libraries. Prior to that, I was a psychology major and a social worker. I have always been fascinated by what makes people tick. While the success of a work of fiction in any genre may depend on the specifics, for me, its true value lies in the universal truths about human experience that it portrays and reveals. In Louise Penny’s words, “crime was deeply human.”.

    Here are seven novels that focus on motive in a variety of ways.

    Agatha Christie, Five Little Pigs.

    No one weaves a mystery from its three strands better than the grande dame of crime fiction, Agatha Christie. In Five Little Pigs, a young woman asks Hercule Poirot to investigate the death of her father for which her mother was convicted sixteen years earlier. The evidence at trial was overwhelming and the accused woman’s defense weak.

    According to recent reports, shortly before her own death, the mother professed her innocence to her child in a letter. Due to the passage of time, Poirot must depend on character, rather than evidence, to solve the case. He says, “[Character] is the principal interest of all my cases.” The “five little pigs” are the five people, other than the wife, who had the opportunity to kill Amyas Crane, a talented but eminently unlikeable painter.

    Initially, none of the five appears to have a motive to murder him. Poirot tells one of the suspects, “the reason for murder is nearly always to be found by a study of the person murdered.” As Poirot delves into the past, he uncovers the truth about Crane’s life and learns that each of the five did, indeed, have a motive. His analysis of the behavior and motivations of several of the suspects ultimately leads him to the solution.

    It has been revealed that more than sixty years after Christie’s novel was published, Louise Penny introduces another wise Francophone inspector, Armande Gamache. He, too, investigates the murder of an artist.

    The puzzle in Still Life is that, unlike Christie’s victim, Jane Neal of the idyllic Quebecois village of Three Pines was beloved by all. When Neal’s body is found in the woods, felled by an arrow, on Thanksgiving morning, Gamage asks, “who would want to kill kindness?” He later explains “most premeditated murders were about rancid emotions, greed, jealousy, fear, all repressed.”.

    Penny introduces us to a host of Three Pines villagers, among whom are both suspects and others who will become fond recurring characters in future books, the twenty-first of which was just published this fall.

    Heather Young, The Distant Dead.

    Sal, a lonely sixth-grade boy, discovers the burned body of middle-school teacher Adam Merkel in the Nevada desert. Merkel had befriended the traumatized boy who came to live on a nearby ranch with his reclusive uncles after the death of his mother.

    In a recent development, when one of Adam’s colleagues, who is dealing with her own personal complications, takes it upon herself to investigate, she uncovers secrets in Adam’s past as she also senses that Sal knows more about Adam’s death than he will admit. Her consideration of possible motives explores how the past and present are immutably intertwined.

    Celeste Ng, Everything I Never Told You.

    It has been revealed that sixteen-year-old Lydia Lee has gone missing. When her body is found in a local lake, her devastated parents need to know how and why it happened. Was it a drowning accident, suicide, or foul play?

    While this moving novel is not a mystery in the traditional sense, it is an exquisite portrayal of how we are shaped by our families and our experiences and how our motives and actions arise from them. As the family’s emotions and secrets long held in silence are slowly and painfully brought to light, we learn the secrets that Lydia, her siblings, her parents, and their parents have harbored, which ultimately reveal Lydia’s fate.

    It has been revealed that this historical legal mystery is set in a small town in 1946 Mississippi. Pete Banning is an upright, church-going model citizen and World War II hero. After returning from the Philippines and the horrors of his war experience there, he hopes to resume the life he left behind with his wife Liza and their children on their cotton farm. When he has Liza committed to a psychiatric hospital and, soon after, calmly shoots his pastor and friend, Dexter Belland, Banning refuses to defend himself, stating only, “I have nothing to say.”.

    Inspired by an actual case from the 1930’s in which the defendant made the same statement until his execution, Grisham keeps the reader guessing until the end why Banning is prepared to die, rather than reveal his motive.

    Anthony Horowitz, The Magpie Murders.

    A murder mystery within a murder mystery. Editor Susan Ryeland receives the manuscript of her client, author Alan Conway’s latest mystery novel featuring detective Atticus Pund, but with the story’s ending missing.

    Recent findings suggest that when Conway is found dead, Ryeland concludes that the manuscript involves real-life events and that Conway’s murderer stole the final pages to avoid incrimination. Ryeland sets out to find the motive and perpetrator of Pund’s fictional mystery to find Conway’s real-life killer.

    Stuart Turton, The 7 ½ Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle.

    Straddling genres, this mystery borrows from speculative fiction to shift time and perspective as the protagonist investigates a murder from the viewpoints of multiple characters within the setting of a classic English country estate. Aiden Bishop wakes up at Blackheath Manor with amnesia and no knowledge of why he is there.

    In each of eight days in a time loop, he finds himself inhabiting a different guest at the manor until he can solve the murder of the young heiress of the estate, Evelyn Hardcastle, who died that evening. If he cannot solve the case by the end of day eight, he is doomed to repeat the cycle with his memory wiped clean.

    Whatever the setting or sub-genre, the key to a murder mystery is motive. As Inspector Armande Gamage put it, “My job is to find people who take lives. And to do that, I have to find out why.”.

    Alice Openshaw has been a fan of mysteries since the age of ten, when she discovered Perry Mason books at her tiny town’s public library. She holds a BA in psychology from Middlebury College in Vermont and an MLS from Vanderbilt University. She lived in rural Maine for thirty years, where she worked as a librarian and adult literacy teacher and raised three children and an assortment of animals on a small farm. She now lives near Cape Cod, Massachusetts, with her husband and her tuxedo cat, Frankie. On the Killer's Trail is her debut novel.

    #32239. Industry News: Catherine Townsend on treating dating like detective work, and vice versa

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1112 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Catherine Townsend on treating dating like detective work, and vice versa

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When I was a dating columnist for The Independent in London, I would often point out the similarities between dating and detective work.
    • Conducting investigative interviews is, in crucial ways, very much like being on one long and strange first date.
    • A more cynical take would be that falling in love is like one long con.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When I was a dating columnist for The Independent in London, I would often point out the similarities between dating and detective work. I’d flag that in both scenarios, you find yourself sitting in front of a stranger—the difference being that in a potential love match, the skeletons in their closet are (hopefully) merely metaphorical, rather than decomposing in a crawl space.

    The same logic works in reverse. Conducting investigative interviews is, in crucial ways, very much like being on one long and strange first date. The idea is to ask open-ended questions and to encourage the person you are trying to get information from to keep talking about themselves. If they keep talking, eventually you can find the inconsistencies in their story.

    A more cynical take would be that falling in love is like one long con. When we like someone, our brain is wired to look for commonalities. And the more we like someone, the more we mimic their behavior. This works extremely well for getting someone to trust you— and that is why con artists mimic our movements, too, for less pure reasons.

    But my job when I’m conducting an interview is to see the worst in people.

    Industry observers note that in 2010, I was living in Los Angeles, had just enrolled in PI school with Dale, and was moonlighting as a PI. State boards give credit to-ward investigative hours for police work, which is why retired police detectives can qualify as licensed private investigators. But, despite the fact that investigative journalism uses a lot of the same skill sets as detective work, journalists are given zero credit for hours worked in newsrooms.

    My first encounters with law enforcement had been less than satisfactory, and I was convinced that this was because, for the most part, they didn’t trust the media. So I wanted to get some more specialized training, something that would raise my skill levels and, hopefully, my esteem in the eyes of the police departments that I was trying to sweet-talk.

    Living in Los Angeles, the quintessential sunny place for shady people, is like having permanent residence inside a noir mystery painted with the rainbow neon sunsets, and traffic jams, of Grand Theft Auto V.

    Dale sent me out on a lot of matrimonial surveillances, and they almost always unfolded in the same way.

    It has been revealed that sometimes, the clients would summon me to their homes. But, following the detective manual logic on interrogations, I preferred to coax the clients into nonthreatening, neutral territory—preferably one that invoked feelings of nostalgia. I found that magic location sliding into a red leatherette booth at Bob’s Major Boy diner in Burbank at sunrise, sipping a ten-ounce mug of Big Boy medium roast, and watching the pink clouds float across an impossibly bright, Monet-meets-vaporwave California sky.

    It has been revealed that after that, things usually get complicated. The client asks me to follow their boyfriend/husband/girlfriend/married boyfriend who also has another girlfriend but has promised that they are his only mistress. (I pretend to ignore the logical fallacies of that argument.) I ask them what they hope to accomplish from a surveillance.

    It has been revealed that I’m honest: I’ll tell them that it’s expensive, uncertain, and a hell of a lot harder than it looks on TV. (If you don’t believe me, try identifying a subject described as “white man in a suit” outside a downtown office building at night from a fuzzy Facebook photo. Bonus points if it’s a rainy winter night and only a few inches of skin are visible!).

    I’ll also ask them why they believe that their loved one has been unfaithful, and often they will tell me something that lets me know that they already know the truth: Maybe they have found a topless selfie of his secretary, or a scrap of lacy women’s underwear in the glove compartment of his Prius.

    I try to always have these conversations over something sweet, which is why I prefer to meet at restaurants. I load the table with strawberry waffles or a banana milkshake with extra maraschino cherries, since bad news goes down easier with a heavy dose of sugar lubricant. Even Cinnabon at the mall food court is better than nothing: Studies show that our animal brains associate the smells of cinnamon and vanilla with comfort and security.

    “Well, it sounds like you already know the answer,” I inevitably say. Why would you think that this is a good person, despite mounting evidence to the contrary?

    Recent findings suggest that before I dig in and disrupt lives, potentially unearthing a truth that could shake the foundations of a person’s existence, I always ask the same question: Do you really want to know? Little white lies can be the glue that holds relationships together. No, you don’t look fat in those white jeans. Yes, you’re the best sex I’ve ever had.

    I make a point of sliding one of my Patrick Bateman-style thick business cards across the table and making a reference to The Matrix: Would they rather take the blue pill and remain blissfully ignorant, or the red pill to see where the rabbit hole, however unpleasant, leads?

    Some people have a compulsive need to know the reality, however brutal and disruptive it will be to their existence, and they will continue to pick it apart like an overeager esthetician digging out blackheads on YouTube. And then there are those who decide that for whatever reason—long marriage, double mortgage, social hierarchy, or something else—they want to stay inside the much happier bubble they have created.

    Before you ask a question that could shatter your reality forever, it’s key to know which camp you fall into. Because once the bubble is pierced, it’s almost impossible to get back in—and if a person chooses to overlook a betrayal, an infidelity, or something worse, lying to themselves afterward can become a full-time job.

    Catherine Townsend is a journalist, private investigator, and podcaster. She is the host of the iHeartMedia podcast Hell and Gone and Red Collar. After beginning her career as a staff writer for Upcoming York Magazine, Catherine moved to London to create The Independent’s very popular “Sleeping Around” dating column. Her articles have appeared in publications including The Atlantic, Elle, New York, GQ, Marie Claire, Cosmopolitan, The Daily Mail, The New York Post, Investigation Discovery, and HuffPost. She became a licensed private investigator in 2013. She is the author of How to Survive a Murder Investigation: A True Story of Death and Danger in the Ozarks.

    Alexander Scott Mercurio, 21, of Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, was sentenced today to 18 years in prison and lifetime supervised release by U.S. District Judge David C. Nye of the District of Idaho for attempting to provide material support and resources to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

    According to court records, Mercurio planned to incapacitate his father with a metal pipe and take his firearms to use in a mass casualty attack on Idaho churches in the name of ISIS. Mercurio also planned to use flame-covered weapons, explosives, knives, and a machete in the attacks. A search of his house revealed that he had butane canisters, lighters, a pair of handcuffs, a knife, and a machete, as well as several firearms belonging to his father. Days before the planned attack, Mercurio stood before an ISIS flag holding a knife and pledged his allegiance to ISIS. The FBI arrested him on April 6, 2024, one day before his planned attack. In addition to his plot to attack Idaho churches, in early 2023, he created an online repository for pro-ISIS content with the purpose of spreading the doctrine of the Islamic State.

    “America’s founders wanted our Nation to be a place where the faithful of any denomination could exercise their religious beliefs freely and without fear of violence,” mentioned Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Alexander Scott Mercurio planned to attack that fundamental freedom by bringing death and destruction to several churches. This sentence shows that the Department of Justice will relentlessly investigate, pursue, and prosecute those who would terrorize and murder Americans for exercising their religious rights.”.

    “The sentencing of Mercurio today sends the clear message that where individuals intend to pursue acts of terrorism against the United States – whether in Coeur d’Alene, or any other community – they will be brought to justice,” noted U.S. Attorney John C. Shirts for the District of Idaho. “Protecting our communities from terrorist activity is always the number one priority of this office and the Department of Justice. I commend the investigation by the FBI, as well as the valuable assistance provided by the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office and the Ada County Sheriff’s Office.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “With today’s sentencing, this individual is being held accountable for pledging allegiance to ISIS and planning an attack on U.S. soil,” remarked Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI works tirelessly to detect and prevent acts of terrorism in order to protect the American people. We will continue to work closely with our law enforcement and Justice Department partners to make sure anyone who participates in terrorist acts faces justice.”.

    The case was investigated by the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force with assistance from the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office and the Ada County Sheriff’s Office.

    It has been revealed that the case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Heather S. Patricco and David G. Robins for the District of Idaho and Trial Attorney Matthew R. Hracho of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

    #32237. Cutting the deadwood with Clive Cussler – my Dad

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1067 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Cutting the deadwood with Clive Cussler – my Dad

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When the opportunity arose to co-write with Clive Cussler, I thought it would be a uniquely fun experience.
    • Sources indicate that I knew Clive as a genial, good-natured man who loved a good laugh.
    • Recent findings suggest that and so it was– until I submitted an early chapter in our first book together.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the opportunity arose to co-write with Clive Cussler, I thought it would be a uniquely fun experience. After all, he was my father.

    Sources indicate that I knew Clive as a genial, good-natured man who loved a good laugh. He was the type of person who expected a lot from himself, but not from others. Growing up, I had ducked household chores as a kid, crashed the family car as a teen, and frittered away college tuition money on pizza and beer, all without incurring any lasting parental disdain. I expected our collaboration on adventure stories to be equally lighthearted and unruffled.

    Recent findings suggest that and so it was– until I submitted an early chapter in our first book together. I had written a scene in which our protagonist, Dirk Pitt, was beaten to a bloody pulp by a nefarious villain. I had crossed a line with Clive’s protagonist, and the curtain of joviality suddenly came crashing down. It was then and there that I realized the man who didn’t take life at all seriously was dead serious about his writing. Clive knew exactly how he wanted his adventure stories crafted, and he was uncompromising about their execution.

    It took me back to when I was six years old, and my father began writing at night and on weekends in my childhood bedroom, which also served as the family den. He had stacks of paperback books on his desk by the likes of Hammond Innes, Donald Hamilton, and Alistair MacLean. Key passages and sections of dialogue were carefully underlined as he studied the contemporary masters of adventure writing like a Rhodes scholar.

    According to recent reports, clive brought that same dedication to research into his own stories. He loved history, and early on began incorporating historical hooks as key elements in his books. But he never made these inclusions lightly; they were always thoroughly researched.

    According to recent reports, in the prologue to Treasure, a Roman legion is attacked by frontier barbarians in 391 A.D. The legionnaires are supported by an historically accurate contingent of Syrian archers and armed with laminated oval shields unique to that particular era of fading Roman dominance. His descriptions of the weaponry, military organization, and battle tactics demonstrated an impressive depth of study.

    Industry observers note that I was a young teen when Clive wrote his breakout bestseller, Raise the Titanic! He threw himself into researching the Titanic, borrowing every library book he could find on the ship. He joined the Titanic Historical Society to obtain its quarterly journals and enlisted me to stay up with him to watch the British production of A Night to Remember on late-night television. Such was his devotion to the topic that when he purchased and built a Revell plastic model of the ship, he manually extended the lengths of the funnels when he discovered they weren’t properly to scale. The joy he took in his research was reflected in his fictional raising of the grand ship and having it complete its maiden voyage to New York.

    It has been revealed that I share his passion for research, finding it one of the more rewarding aspects of writing. We often discussed the delicate balance involved in incorporating detailed research into a story. Knowledge of the fine details and nuances of a subject can add great flavor to a scene, but there’s also a risk of information overload. As writers, we become mini-experts on a topic and feel compelled to share our newfound knowledge. One common pitfall involves describing places we’ve visited. A writer on vacation in Dublin might later incorporate a night at a pub into a chapter scene. Eager to share the experience, she spends two pages describing the weathered wooden floor, the dusty bottles of whiskey lined above the bar, and the clover designs of the cardboard drink coasters on the tables. An atmospheric plunge suddenly turns into a boring travelogue.

    Those of us who co-wrote with Clive were more than familiar with the crossed-out manuscript pages he would return to us when we got carried away with our own exuberant descriptions.

    “Cut out the deadwood,” he would implore. “Make it fly.”.

    Sources indicate that clive always wanted to drive the narrative forward, but he wasn’t averse to expounding in detail at important points in the story. He might explain an ancient mystery in depth, such as the history of Troy and its related archaeological excavations in Trojan Odyssey. Or he might dive deep into describing an advanced technology incorporated into the story. These passages weren’t intended to demonstrate his knowledge, but to educate readers about elements that ultimately mattered to the plot.

    Clive was a product of his time, and that also influenced his outlook on pacing and structure. Going to the movies was a ritual in his childhood, and he religiously attended matinees every Saturday afternoon. The main features were preceded by short movie serials, such as The Hurricane Express, which starred a young John Wayne. I know this because a local Denver television station aired the episodes in the 1970s, and my father watched them every week with a bowl of popcorn, as if he were eight years old again. Each episode was less than twenty minutes long, requiring a quick setup, an action sequence or two, and, of course, an ending cliffhanger. He wrote with that same sort of pacing and visual storytelling in mind. Clive especially relished ending a chapter with a cliffhanger, keeping readers eager to turn the page.

    Ultimately, it was the swashbuckling sense of fun those films imparted that most influenced his approach to writing. He was more interested in entertaining readers than impressing them with his prose, and entertainment always took precedence. Clive wanted his stories to be gripping and fast-paced, of course, but the key ingredient may have been the very quality that defined his own character: a genuine sense of fun.

    Dirk Cussler is the author of Clive Cussler's The Devil's Sea, and coauthor with Clive Cussler of eight previous Dirk Pitt adventures: Black Wind, Treasure of Khan, Arctic Drift, Crescent Dawn, Poseidon's Arrow, Havana Storm, Odessa Sea, and Celtic Empire. He serves as president of NUMA, where he continues his father's legacy of searching for important historical shipwrecks. He lives in Connecticut.
